section.title: The Certainty of God's Promise
section.sectionRationale: After the severe warning, the writer turns to comfort, grounding the readers' hope in the utter reliability of God's promise. God confirmed His pledge to Abraham with an oath, and by two unchangeable things, His promise and His oath, He gives strong encouragement to those who flee to Him. That hope is anchored in Jesus, who has entered the inner sanctuary as our forerunner.
section.thesis: God confirmed His promise to Abraham with an oath, and by these two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, believers have a hope that is a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, reaching into God's very presence where Jesus, our forerunner and high priest forever after Melchizedek, has already entered on our behalf.
section.frameNote: Two movements: God's promise to Abraham sealed by an oath as the pattern of His unchanging purpose; and the resulting hope, an anchor reaching behind the curtain to where Jesus our forerunner has gone ahead of us.

units.label: God's promise, sealed with an oath

verses.text: When God made His {{epangelia|promise}} to Abraham, since He had no one greater to swear by, He swore by Himself,
saying, “I will surely bless you and multiply your descendants.”
And so Abraham, after waiting patiently, obtained the promise.
Men swear by someone greater than themselves, and their {{horkos|oath}} serves as a confirmation to end all argument.
So when God wanted to make the unchanging nature of His purpose very clear to the heirs of the promise, He guaranteed it with an oath.
Thus by two unchangeable things in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us may be strongly encouraged.

units.label: Hope as an anchor behind the curtain

verses.text: We have this hope as an {{ankyra|anchor}} for the soul, firm and secure. It enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain,
where Jesus our {{prodromos|forerunner}} has entered on our behalf. He has become a high priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.

epangelia.gloss: A promise, a pledge freely given. God's promise to Abraham is the model of His reliable word; the heirs of the promise inherit its certainty, for God cannot lie and always keeps what He pledges.

horkos.gloss: An oath, a sworn confirmation. Among people an oath ends all dispute; God, having no one greater, swore by Himself, adding His oath to His promise so that His unchanging purpose would be doubly certain.

ankyra.gloss: An anchor. Hope is pictured as an anchor of the soul, firm and secure, but one that reaches upward and inward, into the very presence of God behind the curtain, where it holds fast to Christ Himself.

prodromos.gloss: A forerunner, one who goes ahead to prepare the way for others to follow. Jesus has entered the inner sanctuary not alone but as our forerunner, guaranteeing that where He has gone His people will come.

basic.context: Coming out of the severe warning, the writer now reassures. He points to God's promise to Abraham, which God backed with an oath, swearing by Himself since there is no one greater. So the readers have two unchangeable things, God's promise and His oath, and God cannot lie. This gives strong encouragement. Their hope is like an anchor, but one that reaches into God's presence, where Jesus has already gone as their forerunner.
basic.hermeneutics: Read this as the counterweight to the warning: the same God who warns also secures His people with a doubly certain word. The anchor image is striking, an anchor not cast down into the sea but up into heaven, fixed on Christ.
basic.originalLanguages: God's epangelia, promise, was sealed with a horkos, oath. The result is hope like an ankyra, anchor, of the soul, reaching where Jesus, our prodromos, forerunner, has entered.
basic.typology: Abraham, who waited patiently and obtained the promise, is the pattern of faith's endurance. The curtain of the tabernacle, behind which only the high priest could go, foreshadows the way now opened by Jesus into God's presence.
basic.christ: Christ is our forerunner who has entered behind the curtain, into God's very presence, as high priest forever after Melchizedek. Our hope is anchored not in a place but in Him, who has gone ahead to secure our arrival.
basic.god: God binds Himself by promise and oath, condescending to our need for certainty. It is impossible for God to lie; His character is the guarantee. He is the God who keeps His word across generations.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 22 records the oath to Abraham. Numbers 23 says God does not lie. Hebrews 9 and 10 develop the way opened behind the curtain.
basic.oneStory: The promise to Abraham, sworn by God Himself, runs through the whole Bible and is secured in Christ, who has entered God's presence ahead of His people to bring them safely home.

context.literary:
Verses 13 to 20 are the second half of a unit that began at 5:11. The rebuke and warning of 5:11 to 6:8 gave way to confidence in 6:9 to 12, and these verses give the reason for that confidence. The opening word 'for' in the Greek links them directly to verse 12, where the readers are told to imitate those who inherit the promises through faith and patience. Abraham is the first of those, and the writer lets him step forward at once.

The passage moves in three small waves. Verses 13 to 15 tell the story: promise, oath, patient waiting, and receiving. Verses 16 and 17 step back to a general principle, that people swear by someone greater and that the oath ends dispute, and apply it to God. Verses 18 to 20 draw out the consequence for the readers and end by naming Jesus.

A word family ties the paragraph together. The word for confirming or making sure appears in verse 16 and again, in its adjective form, in verse 19, where the anchor is 'firm and secure.' Two other words, 'unchangeable' in verses 17 and 18, are the language of what cannot be altered. The writer stacks them so that the reader feels the weight of certainty.

The passage ends with a hinge. The last clause, 'a high priest forever in the order of Melchizedek,' repeats the words with which 5:10 broke off. The writer has gone out through warning and encouragement and comes back to the place he left, ready for 7:1. That gives the section a frame: the Melchizedek theme opens it and closes it, and everything in between is preparation for hearing about him.
context.historical:
The oath of Genesis 22:16 came at the climax of Abraham's life. He had waited some twenty-five years for a son, from his call at the age of seventy-five, Genesis 12:4, to Isaac's birth when he was a hundred, Genesis 21:5. Then God asked for the boy. The oath was spoken after Abraham had shown he would not withhold his only son, Genesis 22:16. For Israel, this was the foundation story of the covenant. Moses appealed to it when Israel sinned at the golden calf, Exodus 32:13, recalling that God had sworn by His very self.

Oaths were a serious matter in the ancient world. An oath called a god to witness and to punish if it was broken, so the party swearing named someone greater. The writer's argument depends on this custom: people swear by a higher authority, but God has none. The Old Testament has Him swearing by Himself in Genesis 22:16, Isaiah 45:23 and Jeremiah 22:5, and by His holiness in Psalm 89:35.

The readers, wavering under pressure, needed this anchor. They had lost property and endured abuse, Hebrews 10:32 to 34. Roman sailors on the Mediterranean knew an anchor as the thing that kept a ship from the rocks when the wind rose, and Acts 27:29 to 40 shows Paul's ship casting anchors in a storm. The picture came readily to a seafaring empire.

The inner sanctuary was equally familiar. Behind the veil of the tabernacle stood the ark, and only the high priest passed through, once a year, Leviticus 16:2. Hebrews will explain it in chapter 9, noting the 'second curtain' in 9:3. For Jewish readers the thought that a believer's hope could enter there was both thrilling and strange.
context.canonical:
Genesis 22:15 to 18 is the only place where God's oath to Abraham is spelled out as an oath, and the New Testament returns to it again and again. Mary's song recalls 'the oath He swore to our father Abraham,' Luke 1:73, and Peter appeals to the covenant in Acts 3:25. Paul builds on it in Galatians 3, where the promise was given to Abraham and his seed, and a human covenant once ratified cannot be cancelled, Galatians 3:15 to 18. Romans 4:20 and 21 says Abraham was fully persuaded that God was able to do what He had promised.

The truth that God cannot lie runs through both Testaments. Numbers 23:19 says God is not a man that He should lie, and 1 Samuel 15:29 says He does not lie or change His mind. Titus 1:2 speaks of the God who cannot lie, who promised before time began. Second Timothy 2:13 says He cannot deny Himself. Hebrews 6:18 draws on all of these.

Within the letter, the oath theme comes back in 7:20 to 22, where the priest of Psalm 110:4 is made 'with an oath,' and Jesus 'has become the guarantee of a better covenant.' The Abrahamic oath and the priestly oath are therefore the two oaths of Scripture on which the argument turns. The image of the inner sanctuary reappears in 9:24 and 10:19 to 20. The word 'hope' is also tied through the letter, 3:6, 7:19, 10:23, and the motif of looking toward what is set before us returns in 12:1 and 2.

Second Corinthians 1:20 gives the New Testament's summary: all the promises of God are 'Yes' in Christ.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer is giving a sceptical or frightened congregation a reason to go on. After the warning of 6:4 to 8 he does not simply say 'try harder.' He gives them a reason that is outside themselves. What matters is not how steadfast they feel, but how steadfast God is. That is why the paragraph spends more words on God's oath than on the reader's response.

He also gives Abraham as a model, because Abraham's life shows that the promise does not come in an afternoon. Abraham had to wait, and the writer's word is a long-suffering one. The point is to prepare the readers for a delay. If the full inheritance does not arrive at once, that does not mean God has forgotten.

The final part of the paragraph is meant to move them from theology to imagination. Hope is an anchor that goes in, not down, behind the curtain, into the very presence where Jesus has gone. The writer wants them to see that the object of their hope is no abstraction but a person who is already there, their forerunner.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of this passage is a description of what God did and a statement of what is true: He swore, He cannot lie, Jesus has entered. The one explicit prescription is implied by verse 18: that those who have fled to Him should take hold of the hope set before them. Everything else is the ground of that act.

Care is needed with two points. First, the passage does not say that every promise in the Bible is addressed to every reader in the same form. It speaks of the promise made to Abraham and of what it means for 'the heirs of the promise,' so it applies to Christians because they are in Christ, Galatians 3:29. Second, the confidence it teaches is a confidence in God, not a guarantee that things will go smoothly. Abraham waited, and the greater part of what was promised he did not live to see, as Hebrews 11:13 says.

What does carry forward is the shape of faith: it holds to a promise that rests on God's character, it waits patiently, and it looks to where Jesus has gone.

debates.question: What are the 'two unchangeable things' in verse 18?

views.label: God's promise and God's oath
views.case: Verse 17 says God 'guaranteed it with an oath,' and the whole paragraph starts from the promise of verse 13. The two things are therefore the promise made to Abraham and the oath that confirmed it. Each is grounded in God's truthfulness, and together they give the doubled certainty the writer describes. This is by far the most common reading.

views.label: God's word and God's character
views.case: Some frame the two things more broadly as God's spoken pledge and His unchanging nature, since the point of the verse is that 'it is impossible for God to lie.' The difficulty is that the context names promise and oath, and the writer says 'by two unchangeable things in which it is impossible for God to lie,' which treats the two things as the means through which His truthfulness is shown, not as the truthfulness itself.

debates.bearing: Either way the point is the same: God has bound Himself doubly, so that those who flee to Him have unshakable ground for hope, since it is impossible for God to lie.

debates.question: In what sense did Abraham 'obtain the promise' in verse 15, when Hebrews 11:13 says the patriarchs died without receiving what was promised?

views.label: He received the first instalment, Isaac
views.case: Abraham waited for a son and received Isaac, and Hebrews 11:11 and 12 says that descendants came from one who was as good as dead. He also received Isaac back from the altar, 11:17 to 19. On this view 'obtained' refers to the beginning of fulfilment, the pledge of the rest.

views.label: He obtained the assurance, not the inheritance
views.case: The oath itself, spoken after the test, was the thing he obtained, a settled certainty. The land and the nations were still future. This fits 11:13, where the patriarchs saw the promises and welcomed them from afar.

views.label: He obtained it in Christ
views.case: A third view holds that the promise was fully received only in Christ, and that Abraham's reception was real because he saw it by faith, as Jesus said Abraham saw His day, John 8:56. Hebrews 11:39 and 40 says the patriarchs did not receive what was promised because God had planned something better for us, so that together with us they would be made perfect.

debates.bearing: The views are not rivals so much as stages. Abraham received enough to sustain faith, and the fullness is still being delivered. For the reader this means that patience is not a failure of the promise but its normal shape.

study.originalLanguages:
The word 'promise' in verse 13 is epangelia, and the letter uses it with unusual frequency, from 4:1 to 11:39. In Hebrews the promise is not a wish or an offer. It is an announcement that binds the speaker, and the writer wants the reader to hear that weight.

The verb for swearing, together with the noun 'oath' in verses 16 and 17, comes from the same family. The writer says God 'interposed' with an oath, in a verb found only here in the New Testament, the verb of a go-between. It is related to the noun for 'mediator' used of Christ in 8:6, 9:15 and 12:24. The verb suggests that God acts almost as a mediator between Himself and His own word, so that the promise is made doubly firm.

In verse 14 the quotation of Genesis 22:17 follows a Hebrew way of speaking: 'blessing I will bless you and multiplying I will multiply you.' In the Hebrew, an infinitive stands beside a finite verb to give emphasis, and the Septuagint carries it over with a participle beside a verb. The BSB turns it into 'I will surely bless.' The doubling is part of the oath's force.

The expression 'to end all argument' in verse 16 translates a word for dispute, which is used again in 7:7 for what is beyond dispute and in 12:3 for opposition from sinners. The oath is the thing that settles argument. The word for 'confirmation' is the noun form of the 'firm' that appears again in the anchor of verse 19.

'Unchangeable' in verses 17 and 18 is a rare word, found only in these two verses in the New Testament. Its meaning is 'not able to be moved to another place.' The word for God's 'purpose' in verse 17 is the term for counsel or settled will, so the writer says that God wished to show the unchanging character of His will.

In verse 18 the readers are described as 'those who have fled' and the purpose is to 'take hold' of the hope. The second verb is the same one used of 'hold firmly' in 4:14. The hope is something 'set before us,' the same verb used of the race set out for us in 12:1 and the joy set before Jesus in 12:2. Hope here is therefore a goal ahead of us, and the verb of holding links it to the earlier summons.

Verse 19 says the anchor 'enters' behind the curtain, in a present participle. The phrase 'the inner sanctuary behind the curtain' matches the Septuagint wording in Leviticus 16:2, 12 and 15. In verse 20 the word 'forerunner' is found only here in the New Testament. The Septuagint uses a related word in Numbers 13:20 for the first ripe grapes of the season, so the sense is of one who goes first and brings the rest after. 'On our behalf' fixes the purpose: His entry is for us.

typology.type: The offering of Isaac and the oath, Genesis 22:1-18
typology.fulfillment: After Abraham was ready to give up his only son, God swore by Himself and confirmed the promise of blessing for all nations. Hebrews 11:17 to 19 says Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead and, 'in a sense,' received Isaac back from death. The correspondence is of a beloved son given up and received back, and of a promise sealed after the offering. In Christ the escalation is that God did not spare His own Son, Romans 8:32, and the promise to the nations is secured through Him. The type falls short because a ram was provided in Isaac's place, while Christ Himself was the offering.

A person who killed someone unintentionally could flee to a city of refuge and be safe from the avenger until trial. Hebrews 6:18 describes believers as 'those who have fled' to take hold of the hope set before them, and the shape of the image is the same: running from danger toward a secure place. The writer does not quote Numbers, so the link is a fair echo rather than a stated type. The escalation is that the refuge is a person in the presence of God, and the safety does not end with the death of a high priest, as in Numbers 35:25, because this priest lives forever.

typology.type: The veil and the inner sanctuary, Leviticus 16:2
typology.fulfillment: Behind the veil stood the ark and the mercy seat, and only the high priest entered, once a year, with blood. Hebrews 6:19 says our hope enters there, and 9:3 to 10 explains the tent's design. Hebrews 10:19 and 20 says the curtain is His body. The correspondence is that the way to God's presence passes through a priest. The escalation is that He has gone in as forerunner, bringing others behind Him, and that the curtain is open. The type falls short because the old sanctuary was a copy, 8:5, and the entering had to be repeated.

The Septuagint uses a form of the word 'forerunner' for the first fruit of the season, and the spies brought back a sample of the land's produce to show what was coming. Hebrews does not draw this link, so it should be treated as an echo of the word. The idea is the same as in 1 Corinthians 15:20, where Christ is the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. A forerunner is not only a scout but a pledge: where He is, the rest will follow. The type falls short because the spies' sample was only a taste, while Jesus has entered the full reality.

study.christ:
Hebrews 6 ends with a name. After nineteen verses of oaths, anchors and curtains, the writer says, almost quietly, 'where Jesus our forerunner has entered on our behalf.' Everything that has been said about God's faithfulness lands on Him. The promise to Abraham was that all nations would be blessed through his offspring, Genesis 22:18, and Paul says the offspring is Christ, Galatians 3:16. The oath given to Abraham is therefore kept in Jesus.

He is called our 'forerunner,' a word that is found only here in the New Testament. A forerunner goes ahead of an army, a ship or a fleet, and makes the way safe for the rest. The word carries a promise that others will follow. In Hebrews the idea is stated in 2:10, where God makes the pioneer of salvation perfect to bring many sons to glory, and in 12:2, where Jesus is the pioneer and perfecter of faith. We are not asked to find our way into the presence of God. He has gone in and holds the way open.

The phrase 'on our behalf' is the center of it. Jesus did not enter as a private person but as our representative, as the high priest on the Day of Atonement represented the nation. Where He is, we are in principle already present, which is why Ephesians 2:6 can say that God seated us with Him in the heavenly places. The anchor of hope is fastened to One who is there.

The last clause, 'a high priest forever in the order of Melchizedek,' unites the oath of promise with the oath of priesthood. Psalm 110:4 says the LORD has sworn and will not change His mind, and Hebrews 7:20 to 22 says Jesus became a priest with an oath and has become the guarantee of a better covenant. The same God who swore to Abraham swore to the Son. That makes Christ the surety of the promise: His priesthood is the sign that the oath will be kept.

Caution is needed so as not to over-allegorise the anchor. The text does not say the anchor is Jesus; it says the hope is an anchor that enters where Jesus is. The picture is of hope fastened to the heavenly sanctuary, and the One in the sanctuary is the reason it holds. Nor should the 'curtain' here be pressed into the later statement that it is His flesh, 10:20, until the argument reaches it.

For the reader, the effect is to turn hope from a feeling into a destination. The Christian does not hope that the Lord might be kind; they hope in the place where their priest and forerunner now sits, and from which He will appear a second time, 9:28.
study.god:
This passage portrays a God who stoops. Verse 13 says that He had no one greater to swear by, and so He swore by Himself. That is an astonishing act of condescension. A king whose word is perfectly good should not need to swear, and yet God does so because His people need help to believe. He adds to His word, not because it is weak, but because we are.

It portrays a God whose purpose is settled. The phrase 'the unchanging nature of His purpose' says that what He has willed will not be undone. Elsewhere the Old Testament says He is not a man that He should change His mind, Numbers 23:19, and Malachi 3:6 says He does not change. The doctrine of immutability, as Hebrews uses it, is not a cold fact but a comfort: the one who promised is the same one who is faithful.

It portrays a God who cannot lie. The text says this plainly, 'it is impossible for God to lie.' It is not that He is forbidden to lie, but that it is against His nature. Titus 1:2 says the same. Here the truthfulness of God is the basis for hope. If He could lie, the oath would be only a pledge. Because He cannot, it is a rock.

It portrays a God who gives heirs a share of what He has promised. The 'heirs of the promise' of verse 17 are the family of Abraham, and in Christ they are Gentiles as well as Jews, Galatians 3:29. God's purpose is not only to keep His word to one man but to make a family that inherits.

It portrays a God who welcomes. The readers are those who have 'fled' to take hold of hope. God has provided a refuge in His own presence, and the sanctuary behind the curtain is open because Jesus has entered. The God who once barred the way with cherubim, Genesis 3:24, now has a forerunner within the veil.

It also shows the Father's patience with His people. Abraham waited, and God took him through the waiting. The Father does not hurry the fulfilment, and He does not forget.

For worship, the right response is trust and thanksgiving. We can sing to a God whose word holds, and pray with the confidence that He has bound Himself to keep it. The anchor is not our grip on God but His grip on us, since He has sworn and cannot lie.

crossReferences.note: The oath itself. After Abraham did not withhold his only son, God declared 'By Myself I have sworn' and promised blessing, many descendants and blessing for all nations. Hebrews 6:14 quotes the heart of it and reads it as the pattern of God's reliability.

The original promise made when Abraham was called, with its three parts of land, nation and blessing for all the families of the earth. It is the promise whose long waiting the writer has in mind when he says Abraham waited patiently.

A smoking firepot and a flaming torch pass between the halves of the carcasses as the LORD makes a covenant with Abram. Many readers see God taking the covenant curse on Himself, which stands behind the idea that He binds Himself, as Hebrews 6:17 says.

Moses reminds God that He swore to Abraham, Isaac and Israel by His very self. It shows that the oath of Genesis 22 was understood in Israel as a lasting ground on which to plead, as the readers of Hebrews are invited to do.

God is not a man that He should lie or change His mind, and He does not promise without fulfilling. It supplies the Old Testament basis for the claim that it is impossible for God to lie, Hebrews 6:18.

The LORD has sworn and will not change His mind: 'You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.' The second oath, whose words close Hebrews 6:20, links the Abrahamic promise to the priesthood of Christ.

Jesus became a priest with an oath, unlike the Levitical priests, and so became the guarantee of a better covenant. It develops the final clause of 6:20 and shows why the oath matters for the believer's security.

The warning to Aaron not to enter behind the veil freely or he would die. The words of Hebrews 6:19 recall this restricted sanctuary, and so make the point that hope now enters where only the high priest once could.

Believers have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, and are told to hold to the hope they profess because He who promised is faithful. It restates 6:18 to 20 as an invitation.
Abraham did not waver through disbelief but was fully persuaded that God was able to do what He had promised. It shows what the patient waiting of Hebrews 6:15 looked like from the inside.
All the promises of God are 'Yes' in Christ, and through Him our 'Amen' is spoken. The verse names Jesus as the one in whom the promises and oaths of Hebrews 6 are confirmed.
The race is set before us and Jesus is the pioneer and perfecter of faith. The same verb that describes the hope 'set before us' in 6:18 appears here, so hope and race are two sides of one pursuit.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story is held together by promises, and Hebrews 6:13 to 20 explains why that thread can bear weight. Genesis 3 ended with a promise that a seed of the woman would crush the serpent, and then a long silence. Genesis 12 gave the promise a name and a family: all the families of the earth would be blessed through Abraham. Genesis 22 sealed it with an oath. Everything that follows in the Old Testament is the history of that oath being kept against the odds, through barren wombs, slavery, wilderness and exile.

Israel's story shows why the oath was needed. Moses pleaded it at Sinai, Exodus 32:13. The prophets recalled it when the nation was in ruins. Micah ends by saying that God will show faithfulness to Jacob and loyalty to Abraham, as He swore, Micah 7:20. God keeps swearing because people keep forgetting.

The coming of Christ is the point where promise and oath become flesh. He is the offspring in whom the blessing is for all nations, Galatians 3:16, and He is the priest whom God swore to appoint, Psalm 110:4. The anchor of Hebrews 6:19 is therefore not set in a hope that might come true, but in a person who has already come and gone ahead.

That puts the church in the middle of the story. Believers have been given a down payment and a pledge, but they still wait. Like Abraham, they are called to patience. They are also told what to do while they wait: hold to the hope, which is firm because it is fastened behind the curtain.

The new creation is the full arrival of the promise. Revelation 21:3 hears a voice from the throne saying that God's dwelling is with humanity, and Revelation 22:3 to 5 says His servants will see His face. What began in a garden with a promise of a seed ends in a city with the forerunner's people gathered in. The oath has been kept to the last word, and the anchor has found its harbour.

quiz.q: Why did God swear by Himself when making His promise to Abraham?

options.text: Because there was no one greater to swear by.
Because His word alone was unreliable.
options.note: God's word is fully reliable; the oath was a condescension to our need for certainty.
The oath displays God's purpose to reassure the heirs, not a response to a demand.

options.text: To give the heirs of the promise stronger encouragement.
options.note: This is the purpose of the oath in verse 17, but the reason He swore by Himself specifically is that there was no one greater.

quiz.q: What are the two unchangeable things that give believers strong encouragement?

options.text: God's promise and God's oath, in which it is impossible for Him to lie.
options.note: Verses 17 to 18 name the promise and the confirming oath.
The two things are God's promise and oath, not law and temple.

options.text: God's word and God's unchanging character.
options.note: This is close, since both rest on God's truthfulness, but the two things the passage names are the promise and the confirming oath.
The encouragement rests on God's promise and oath, not on human faith itself.

quiz.q: What image describes the believer's hope, and where does it reach?

options.text: An anchor of the soul reaching behind the curtain into God's presence.
options.note: Verse 19 pictures hope as an anchor entering the inner sanctuary.

options.text: A shield that keeps God at a distance.
options.note: Hope is an anchor drawing us to God, not a shield against Him.

options.text: An anchor cast down into the depths of the sea.
options.note: This anchor reaches upward into heaven, not down into the sea.

options.text: An anchor, firm and secure, holding the soul steady.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but the passage's striking point is that this anchor reaches upward behind the curtain into God's presence.

quiz.q: What does it mean that Jesus is our 'forerunner'?

options.text: He has entered God's presence ahead of us, guaranteeing we will follow.
options.note: Verse 20 calls Him the forerunner who entered on our behalf.

options.text: He went ahead but we can never follow.
options.note: A forerunner goes ahead precisely so others will follow.

options.text: He is merely an example, unconnected to us.
options.note: He acts on our behalf, not merely as a distant example.

options.text: He has entered God's presence on our behalf as our representative.
options.note: True and central, but the idea of forerunner adds that He goes ahead so that we will follow where He has gone.

questions: God bound Himself by promise and oath to reassure us. Where do you need to rest more fully on the certainty that God cannot lie?
Abraham obtained the promise after waiting patiently. How is God growing patient endurance in you as you wait on His promises?
Our hope is an anchor reaching into God's presence. What storms in your life is that anchor holding you steady through?
Jesus has gone ahead as our forerunner. How does it change your view of the future to know He has secured your place with God?
We are those who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us. What does it look like to keep fleeing to Christ as your refuge?

translationNotes.note: The quotation is from Genesis 22:17, God's oath after the offering of Isaac; the doubled Greek construction, 'surely bless', renders the emphatic Hebrew idiom of certainty.
The anchor imagery is unusual in that it reaches upward, into the inner sanctuary; the hope is fixed not below in the sea but above in God's presence.
'Forerunner' translates prodromos, a term for a scout or advance runner; it stresses that Jesus entered God's presence not only for Himself but to open the way for His people to follow.
